models.title: Cause-and-effect analysis
models.principle: Coming first is not causing. Check common causes, reverse causation and chance, and ask what evidence would settle it.

steps.title: The claim
steps.prompt: Write the cause-and-effect claim: A leads to B.

steps.title: Check it
steps.prompt: Which of these could be going on?
options: I only know A came before B
A third factor could cause both
Someone could change A and watch B

steps.title: Other explanations
steps.prompt: List other things that could explain B.

steps.title: Evidence that would settle it
steps.prompt: What would you need to see?

steps.title: Your judgment
steps.prompt: For now, I think…

rules.say: You only know the order but judged it causal — order alone is not evidence.
You named other explanations and the evidence that would decide — that is the core of a causal analysis.

models.limits: Good for empirical claims. It does not answer philosophical questions about what causation is.

models.title: Systems thinking (feedback loops)
models.principle: Outcomes often come from loops: parts that affect each other in circles. Reinforcing loops amplify, balancing loops hold things steady.

steps.title: Parts
steps.prompt: List the parts or quantities involved (at least 2).

steps.title: Links
steps.prompt: Connect parts: when the first goes up, does the second go up (+) or down (−)?

steps.title: Where to intervene
steps.prompt: Which link or part would you change, and why?

rules.say: Look at the loops below: a loop with an even number of ‘−’ links is reinforcing, an odd number is balancing.

models.limits: A loop diagram is a simplification; real systems have delays and more parts than any sketch.

models.title: Incentive analysis
models.principle: People respond to what they are rewarded and punished for — which may differ from what a rule intends.

steps.title: Intended goal
steps.prompt: What is the rule or plan supposed to achieve?

steps.title: Who is involved
steps.prompt: List the people or groups affected.

steps.title: What each actor wants and is rewarded for
steps.prompt: Fill in what you can.

steps.title: Mismatch
steps.prompt: Where does what people are rewarded for differ from the goal?

rules.say: Compare the rows: the same rule can push different actors in different directions.

models.limits: People also act from values, habits and identity, not only incentives.

models.title: Multiple perspectives
models.principle: The same issue looks different from different standpoints. Laying them side by side shows what each one notices and misses.

steps.title: The issue
steps.prompt: State the issue or question.

steps.title: Perspectives
steps.prompt: Add 2–4 standpoints (people, groups or theories).

steps.title: Compare
steps.prompt: What does each perspective see and value?

steps.title: What I take from this
steps.prompt: Where do they agree or clash, and where do you stand now?

rules.say: Three or more perspectives — check whether one of them is one you disagree with.

models.limits: Choosing which perspectives to include already shapes the result.

models.title: Socratic definition
models.principle: Propose a definition, test it against examples and counterexamples, and revise it.

steps.title: First definition
steps.prompt: X is…

steps.title: Examples
steps.prompt: Cases that fit your definition and really are X.

steps.title: Counterexamples
steps.prompt: Cases that fit the definition but are not X — or are X but don’t fit.

steps.title: Revised definition
steps.prompt: Improve the definition to handle the counterexamples.

rules.say: You found a counterexample — try revising the definition.
Definition revised after a counterexample. You can test the new one again.

models.limits: Some concepts may not have a neat definition at all; that can be a finding too.

models.title: Necessary & sufficient conditions
models.principle: A necessary condition must hold for something to be X; a sufficient condition guarantees it is X. Test them on cases.

steps.title: Necessary conditions
steps.prompt: Without these, it can’t be X.

steps.title: Sufficient conditions
steps.prompt: If these hold, it is definitely X.

steps.title: Test cases
steps.prompt: Add cases; mark whether they meet your conditions and whether they really are X.

rules.say: At least one case doesn’t match — your conditions need another look.

models.limits: Many everyday concepts work by family resemblance rather than strict conditions.
